narrative:
The model determined that you have a 70% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three pieces of information about you drove that outcome, ranked from most to least influential. First, your LSAT score of 32 sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted. This was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Second, your family income being in the middle bracket also increased the chance of failure, though less dramatically; among accepted students this bracket is fairly common but still contributed a negative signal. Third, your third-year grades were actually helpful: placing in the 8th decile outperformed the average of roughly 5.8 among accepted students and pulled the prediction back toward passing.

In short, the lower LSAT score outweighed your solid later academic performance and created too much risk in the model’s eyes. Gender and race played no role in this decision.

What you should do next is retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score. Improving that one area would likely shift your predicted probability enough to make future applications competitive.
